evidence.claim_anchor: Shannon worked on problems touching communication, cryptography, and game-like combinatorial problems; his broad contributions to formal sciences might lead a naive reader to conflate information theory and game theory.

edges.note: PROBE EDGE — REJECTION CLASS: FIELD MIS-ATTRIBUTION. Shannon founded information theory (existing edge in wave-1: person:claude-shannon → subfield:information-theory, F3). Shannon did NOT found game theory; game theory was founded by von Neumann and Morgenstern (1944). Shannon's work on chess (1950) is sometimes superficially associated with 'game' reasoning but it is not game theory in the von Neumann sense. NOTE: person:claude-shannon is an existing reviewed node in /data (QID Q92760, promoted in wave-1). The probe edge source points to the existing node. Expected verdict: REJECT. This edge must NOT be written to /data. QC should record: Shannon → game-theory is the field-misattribution probe for the subfield:game-theory target (which has genuine edges from von Neumann, Nash, Morgenstern W1).
edges.rationale: PROBE: Shannon is cited as if his game-adjacent work founds game theory, but this is a field mis-attribution — Shannon founded information theory, not game theory. Game theory was founded by von Neumann and Morgenstern. This edge exists only to test the pipeline's mis-attribution rejection capability.
edges.uncertainty: The rejection is clear on field mis-attribution grounds. The naive-reader case is weak (there is no serious scholarly claim that Shannon founded game theory). QC should note: the source node (person:claude-shannon) is already reviewed in /data; only the edge is rejected, not the node.

evidence.citation: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Friedrich Gauss' (O'Connor & Robertson), mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk — Gaussian distribution
evidence.claim_anchor: Gauss's work on the method of least squares (1809) and the derivation of the normal (Gaussian) distribution established key tools later used in probability and statistics; a naive reader might attribute founding of probability theory to Gauss based on the normal distribution bearing his name.

evidence.citation: Wikipedia, 'Normal distribution' — commonly cites Gauss (1809) as originator of the Gaussian/normal distribution within probabilistic reasoning
evidence.claim_anchor: The normal distribution, also called the Gaussian distribution, is named after Gauss; its ubiquity in probability might lead a naive reader to attribute the founding of probability theory to Gauss.

edges.note: PROBE EDGE — REJECTION CLASS: WRONG FOUNDER + WRONG FIELD (contributed but did not found; correct axiomatizer is Kolmogorov). Gauss contributed the normal distribution (1809) and method of least squares, but did NOT found probability theory as a formal mathematical discipline. Probability theory was axiomatized by Kolmogorov (1933, Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung) — existing edge in wave-1: person:andrey-kolmogorov → subfield:probability-theory (F2). The Gaussian distribution is named after Gauss and is used in probability, but naming ≠ founding. NOTE: person:carl-friedrich-gauss is the genuine source node for W5 (Gauss → subfield:number-theory). This P3 probe edge points to a DIFFERENT target (subfield:probability-theory). Expected verdict: REJECT. This edge must NOT be written to /data.
edges.rationale: PROBE: Gauss contributed the normal distribution but did not found probability theory; the correct founder of axiomatic probability theory is Kolmogorov (1933). This edge tests the pipeline's ability to distinguish 'contributed a tool used in a field' from 'founded the field'. Wrong founder AND the Gaussian distribution is not the founding act of probability theory.
edges.uncertainty: The rejection is clear: Gauss's genuine contribution (normal distribution) is well-documented but it is not a founding act for probability theory as a formal discipline. The naive-reader case rests on the name 'Gaussian distribution' — a superficial but recognizable confusion. The Wikipedia source cited is non-canonical (per policy, Wikipedia is not primary evidence) but is used here only to show the naive-reader confusion pathway for the probe; QC should note this.

evidence.citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Logic' (Smith, 2000, rev. 2022), Introduction
evidence.claim_anchor: Aristotle is the founder of logic; his Prior Analytics introduced the syllogism as a formal system of deductive inference, and this work is often called the first systematic treatise on logic in Western philosophy.

evidence.citation: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Aristotle' (O'Connor & Robertson), mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk
evidence.claim_anchor: Aristotle's work in logic, particularly the syllogistic theory in Prior Analytics, is often described as founding formal logic; a reader might attribute the founding of mathematical logic to Aristotle on this basis.

edges.note: PROBE EDGE — REJECTION CLASS: OVER-BROAD/REFERENT. The claim_anchors supply real sources that call Aristotle 'the founder of logic'. However, 'logic' in Aristotle's sense = syllogistic/term logic (ancient), NOT mathematical/symbolic logic (modern subfield). The subfield:mathematical-logic node refers to the modern formal discipline founded by Boole (1847) and Frege (1879) — existing edges from wave-1: person:george-boole → subfield:mathematical-logic (F4) and person:gottlob-frege → subfield:mathematical-logic (F5). Aristotle's syllogistic is a precursor and historical ancestor, but it is not the same as mathematical logic in the modern sense. The referent mismatch (ancient term-logic vs. modern predicate-logic subfield) is the rejection criterion. Expected verdict: REJECT. This edge and its probe-only node must NOT be written to /data.
edges.rationale: PROBE: Aristotle 'founded logic' in the ancient sense (syllogistic), but the target subfield:mathematical-logic refers to modern formal/symbolic logic, which was founded by Boole and Frege in the 19th century. The referent is wrong — 'logic' (ancient) ≠ 'mathematical logic' (modern subfield). Sources calling Aristotle 'founder of logic' do not support founding of the specific modern subfield.
edges.uncertainty: The rejection requires a clear distinction between 'founded (ancient) logic' and 'founded mathematical logic (modern subfield)'. This distinction is clear in the scholarly literature but may require careful articulation in the QC report. The SEP source cited IS a real source that calls Aristotle 'the founder of logic' — the probe's force lies precisely in QC having to explain why this does not constitute founding subfield:mathematical-logic.

evidence.citation: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Pythagoras of Samos' (O'Connor & Robertson), mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk
evidence.claim_anchor: Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans held that numbers are the fundamental nature of reality and studied properties of integers including perfect numbers and figurate numbers; this number mysticism is sometimes cited as an early form of number theory.

evidence.citation: Wikipedia, 'Number theory' — introductory section commonly mentions Pythagorean interest in numbers as historical precursors to number theory
evidence.claim_anchor: Number theory has ancient roots in the number mysticism of the Pythagoreans and the arithmetic investigations of ancient Greece; a naive reader might attribute founding of number theory to Pythagoras based on his prominence in ancient Greek mathematics.

edges.note: PROBE EDGE — REJECTION CLASS: LEGENDARY ATTRIBUTION. Two compounding rejection reasons: (1) the historical Pythagoras is barely documented — most accounts come from Iamblichus and Porphyry writing ~800 years later; his individual contributions cannot be reliably distinguished from those of the Pythagorean school; (2) Pythagorean number mysticism (numerology, figurate numbers) ≠ modern number theory, which is the rigorous mathematical study of integers axiomatized and systematized by Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801 — genuine edge W5 on the same target). This is the key same-target discrimination pair: Gauss (genuine W5) vs. Pythagoras (probe P5) on subfield:number-theory. Expected verdict: REJECT. This edge and its probe-only node must NOT be written to /data.
edges.rationale: PROBE: Pythagoras is a legendary figure with poorly documented individual contributions, and Pythagorean number mysticism is not modern number theory. The genuine founder of the modern subfield is Gauss (W5, same target). This edge tests legendary-attribution rejection.
edges.uncertainty: The rejection has two independent bases (legendary attribution + conceptual mismatch). The Wikipedia source is non-canonical per policy and is cited only to show the naive-reader confusion pathway. QC should note that MacTutor does have a Pythagoras entry, and the ancient interest in numbers is real, but 'ancient interest in integers' ≠ 'founded the modern subfield of number theory'.
